text: Pig disease recognition means noticing changes from normal behavior, not diagnosing from one symptom. African swine fever (ASF; ជំងឺប៉េស្តជ្រូកអាហ្វ្រិក) can cause high fever, depression, vomiting, diarrhea, skin redness/hemorrhages, abortion, and sudden death with extremely high mortality in severe outbreaks. Classical swine fever (CSF) produces overlapping signs -- fever, huddling, weakness, conjunctivitis, digestive upset, unsteady movement, sometimes purplish skin discoloration. CRITICALLY, ASF and CSF look very similar and cannot be reliably told apart by symptoms alone -- never tell a farmer a pig 'definitely has' ASF or CSF based only on signs. Foot-and-mouth disease causes fever, salivation, mouth/foot lesions, and severe lameness. Swine dysentery causes progressively severe diarrhea with mucus and sometimes blood, dehydration, and poor growth -- but bloody diarrhea alone doesn't confirm it, since other conditions cause similar signs. Respiratory disease may show as coughing, nasal discharge, and difficult breathing. During the wet season, watch mud, standing water, and contaminated equipment; during the dry season, watch heat stress, dust, and dehydration -- but don't use environmental conditions to diagnose a specific disease. For smallholder pigs with simple pens and limited biosecurity, the practical response to sudden unexplained deaths, rapidly spreading illness, high fever with hemorrhagic signs, severe bloody diarrhea, or multiple sick animals is: minimize movement and sales immediately, separate affected animals where feasible, avoid moving equipment between pens, and contact a veterinarian or animal-health authority for urgent investigation.
